group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
An 84-year-old man who still drives himself to the local senior center for weekly bridge games was brought to the emergency department by his daughter after three days of progressively wetter cough, low-grade rigors, and an early-morning fever surge that touched 38.7 °C on an oral thermometer at home; he purposefully declined the acetaminophen and short-acting inhaler his primary care physician had prescribed years earlier for episodic bronchospasm, explaining that he preferred the hospital staff “see the numbers unaltered.” He walked from the curb into triage without supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, or antimicrobial therapy. Past history is notable for long-standing diabetic-hypertensive nephropathy now classified as stage-4 chronic kidney disease with an estimated glomerular filtration rate in the mid-20s; he follows nephrology quarterly, keeps a strict low-salt diet, and has never required renal replacement therapy. There is no record of prior stroke, transient ischemic attack, malignancy, chronic liver disorder, or residence in any institutional setting; he lives alone in a split-level home, climbs the eight interior steps twice daily, and performs his own grocery shopping. He quit a 15-pack-year cigarette habit four decades ago, drinks a single glass of red wine every Sunday, and denies recreational drug use. Immunization registry confirms completion of both pneumococcal formulations and this season’s inactivated influenza vaccine. Upon roll-in he sat erect on the stretcher, answered questions coherently, identified the date, location, and current president, and recalled three objects at five minutes, indicating intact cognition. Skin was warm and lightly diaphoretic with capillary refill under two seconds; no peripheral edema or scleral icterus was noted. Untreated triage vitals on room air at this sea-level facility were: oral temperature 38.65 °C, a rapid regular radial pulse of 141 beats min⁻¹ confirmed on telemetry as sinus tachycardia, automated right-arm blood pressure 155/79 mm Hg verified manually, respirations counted for a full minute at 29 breaths min⁻¹ with mild supraclavicular activity, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 95 % and 96 %. Neck veins were not distended above the clavicle at 45°, and no carotid bruits were appreciated. Cardiac auscultation revealed a brisk S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The lung examination demonstrated markedly diminished breath sounds with stony dull percussion and a subtle superior meniscus over the lower half of the left posterior thorax, while coarse inspiratory crackles peppered the adjacent parenchyma; the right lung transmitted vesicular sounds throughout without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and nondistended with normal bowel sounds and no organomegaly. A brief neurologic screen revealed equal reactive pupils, symmetric strength, steady finger-nose testing, and normal gait when he stood momentarily. Bedside glucometer prior to venipuncture read 139 mg dL⁻¹. Venous chemistry drawn within ten minutes of arrival, before any saline flush larger than 2 mL, returned sodium 109 mEq L⁻¹, potassium 4.2 mEq L⁻¹, chloride 86 mEq L⁻¹, bicarbonate 15 mEq L⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 68 mg dL⁻¹, and serum creatinine 2.9 mg dL⁻¹, consistent with his usual chronic impairment but notable for pronounced hyponatremia and azotemia. Complete blood count showed leukocytes 13.8 × 10⁹ L⁻¹ with 88 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 46 %, hemoglobin 15.1 g dL⁻¹, and platelet count 240 × 10⁹ L⁻¹. A right radial arterial sample obtained while he remained on ambient air demonstrated pH 7.13, PaCO₂ 29 mm Hg, PaO₂ 111 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 10 mEq L⁻¹, indicating a primary metabolic acidosis with compensatory hyperventilation and preserved oxygen tension. Serum lactate measured 2.1 mmol L⁻¹, and high-sensitivity troponin I was below the assay threshold. Point-of-care capillary ketones were negative. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph acquired before any antimicrobial, crystalloid, or analgesic administration revealed dense consolidation occupying the lingula and lower lobe of the left lung with conspicuous air bronchograms plus a concave fluid layer that obliterated the left costophrenic angle, consistent with a moderate pleural collection; heart size and mediastinum were unremarkable for age, and vertebral bodies showed mild osteopenia. Thoracic ultrasound at bedside confirmed an anechoic stripe approximately 3 cm in depth posteriorly with dynamic air bronchograms in the neighboring parenchyma. Twelve-lead electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 142 beats min⁻¹ with left-ventricular voltage criteria and nonspecific ST-T wave flattening unchanged from a tracing six months earlier. Two peripheral sets of blood cultures, a nurse-assisted expectorated sputum sample, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, and a multiplex respiratory viral panel were dispatched to the laboratory before any antibiotics or supportive medications were ordered. Up to the moment this narrative is entered he has received no intravenous fluids, vasopressors, bronchodilators, corticosteroids, diuretics, antipyretics, or supplemental oxygen beyond minimal heparinized saline used to maintain the arterial catheter, ensuring that every vital sign, laboratory result, and imaging finding above reflects his untreated presentation physiology.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation:
- Demographics: a man's baseline score is his age → 84. He lives at home, so nursing-home residence adds 0.
- Comorbidities: stage-4 chronic kidney disease → 10. No documented malignancy, liver disease, heart failure, or cerebrovascular disease → 0 each.
- Examination: pulse 141/min (≥125) → 10. He is oriented, RR 29 is below 30/min, systolic BP 155 is not <90 mm Hg, and temperature 38.65°C is neither <35°C nor ≥40°C → 0 each.
- Laboratory findings: arterial pH 7.13 (<7.35) → 30; BUN 68 mg/dL (≥30) → 20; sodium 109 mEq/L (<130) → 20. Glucose 139 mg/dL (<250), hematocrit 46% (not <30%), and PaO₂ 111 mm Hg (not <60) → 0 each.
- Imaging: left pleural effusion → 10.
Sum: 84 + 10 + 10 + 30 + 20 + 20 + 10 = 184.
Final answer: 184
